shared.title: Probability exam: interpreting conditions before calculating
shared.acceptedOutcome: Prepare for the 20 October introductory probability assessment by solving and explaining conditional probability, tree-based total probability and Bayes problems, and distinguishing independence from mutually exclusive events, within the confirmed study time.

student.profile: Nadia, a first-year university student, has attended the probability lectures. This is one course alongside other commitments, not a request for a complete degree study programme.
student.goal: Aim for at least 75% on the upcoming assessment; treat this as a target, not a promised result. I particularly want to stop reversing the conditioning and to explain why a denominator is appropriate.
student.preferences: Use manageable sessions, usually around 20 minutes and never more than 30 minutes without a break. I prefer moderate effort and essential work comfortably before the deadline when feasible, keeping room for actual gaps. I learn from worked examples followed by trying a changed problem without looking at the solution. I dislike copying lecture notes. I can use pen, paper and a basic calculator.
student.acceptedRequest: Make a complete, realistic preparation plan for this assessment using my observed errors and the supplied resources. Prioritize the gaps that actually matter, preserve a modest check of secure material if justified, and leave spare time unused when extra work would not help. Explain what I should do if a checkpoint shows I am still confused. No work on exam day or my unavailable days.

assessment.format: Closed-book, 40 minutes, basic calculator allowed. The teacher's supplied outline lists conditional probability from tables, two-stage tree problems, Bayes calculations and explanations of independence versus mutually exclusive events. Actual exam questions and topic mark weights have not been released.
assessment.provenance: Synthetic course scenario. The outline below is an accepted student-supplied handout for this experiment, not a verified official external assessment. No claims about unreleased questions or weights are authorized.

readiness.statement: On 9 October I answered 4/4 simple unconditional counting questions and 3/3 fraction-to-decimal questions correctly, unaided. On the supplied 200-person table I answered P(train | late)=24/80, mixing up the denominator; I could correct it to 24/40 after the tutor explicitly pointed out the conditioning group. I have not yet demonstrated that correction unaided on a changed table.
On 9 October I multiplied probabilities along one branch correctly in 2/2 attempts but missed the second contributing branch in one total-probability question. There is no timed mixed-test evidence.

On 9 October I gave 0.9 for P(Box A | red) in the two-box question, quoting P(red | Box A). I could follow the tutor's numerator and total-probability denominator afterwards, but have not solved a new Bayes problem independently.
On 9 October I described two disjoint nonzero-probability events as independent because they do not overlap. I have no subsequent evidence correcting that explanation.

resources.name: Available tutor handout: rules and actual practice problems
resources.content:
Rules: P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0. For mutually exclusive exhaustive groups G1,G2, P(R)=P(G1)P(R|G1)+P(G2)P(R|G2). Bayes reverses a conditioning using joint probability over the appropriate total. Independence means P(A and B)=P(A)P(B). Mutually exclusive means P(A and B)=0.
Problem 1: Among 200 students, 80 travel by train and 120 otherwise. Of the train group 24 were late; of the other group 16 were late. Find P(late), P(train|late), and P(late|train), explaining each denominator.
Problem 2: Box A is selected with probability 0.2 and contains 9 red and 1 blue tokens. Box B is selected with probability 0.8 and contains 2 red and 8 blue tokens. One token is drawn from the selected box. Find P(red) and P(Box A|red), and explain why the latter is not 0.9.
Problem 3: Repeat the box problem with P(Box A)=0.5, keeping the box contents unchanged; explain how the answer changes.
Problem 4: A fair six-sided die is rolled. A={1,2,3}, B={4,5,6}, C={2,4,6}. Decide whether A,B are independent and whether A,C are independent; show the relevant probabilities.
These are practice problems, not the unreleased assessment. New practice examples may be constructed and must be identified as new.

resources.name: Available tutor solution key
resources.content: Problem 1: P(late)=40/200=0.2; P(train|late)=24/40=0.6; P(late|train)=24/80=0.3. Problem 2: P(red)=0.2*0.9+0.8*0.2=0.34; P(Box A|red)=0.18/0.34=9/17, approximately 0.5294. Problem 3: P(red)=0.55; P(Box A|red)=0.45/0.55=9/11, approximately 0.8182. Problem 4: A and B each have probability 1/2, their intersection is empty, so they are mutually exclusive and not independent. A and C each have probability 1/2 but P(A and C)=1/6, not 1/4, so they are not independent. The key is available to check work afterwards; reading it is not evidence of unaided mastery.
